title: Verifier‑Assisted vs. LLM‑Only Pre‑deployment Network‑Change Validation: A Confirmatory Paired Study
abstract: We evaluated whether integrating a deterministic pre‑deployment verifier into an LLM‑driven change‑generation pipeline increases the fraction of intent‑driven configuration proposals that pass semantic validation (unflagged verifier pass) relative to single‑shot LLM generation. Following a preregistered paired design (cnsmp2026-llm-verifier-predeployment-001; preregistration SHA‑256 = 425cb1652354120cf48f686b964723d64c76d0a8abe53cd5b5ad0eaa1af71fc7), we executed 300 paired intent tasks (100 per complexity stratum: low/medium/high) using gpt-5-mini and a deterministic NetOps validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5). For each pair a single shared LLM generation was produced and then evaluated under two conditions: baseline = accept single‑shot output; guarded = verifier + up to one automated repair. Observed outcomes: baseline unflagged pass 299/300 (0.9967), guarded 300/300 (1.0000); absolute paired difference = 0.00333; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; 95% paired bootstrap percentile CI = [0.00, 0.01] (bootstrap_seed=1729, B=10000). The preregistered pilot (n=60) was not executed; the main N=300 was used as pre‑specified. The preregistered primary hypothesis (≥10 percentage‑point paired improvement) was not supported because baseline performance was near ceiling on this synthetic suite. We report the frozen design, complete execution artifacts, per‑stratum outcomes, contamination checks, and deterministic analysis, and discuss implications for evaluating verifier utility under more challenging and diverse conditions.

sections.introduction: Generative large language models (LLMs) are being applied to NetOps tasks such as intent→configuration translation, template synthesis, and automated repair. Prior work shows tool‑augmented architectures and generate→validate→repair patterns can reduce syntactic and semantic errors, motivating verifier integration in pre‑deployment workflows. Yet the marginal operational benefit of adding a verifier depends on base generation quality, task difficulty, and validator coverage. We preregistered and executed a confirmatory paired experiment to measure that marginal effect under a controlled synthetic NetOps suite. Research question: Does a verifier‑assisted pipeline increase the fraction of change proposals that pass semantic pre‑deployment validation (unflagged) compared to single‑shot LLM generation? Contributions: (1) a preregistered paired evaluation (N=300 pairs) using a shared‑generation protocol; (2) full archival of execution and analysis artifacts; (3) a measured outcome showing negligible paired improvement on the supplied synthetic benchmark and a discussion of construct and external validity implications.
sections.related_work: Surveys and recent system papers document active research into LLMs for network configuration, intent translation, tool‑augmented agents, and generate→validate→repair patterns. Representative works include intent translation and template synthesis systems, planner‑centric tool frameworks, and studies that report correctness gains when validators are integrated. Hallucination‑detection and deterministic safety‑net approaches further motivate verifiers for high‑stakes operational tasks. However, prior reports are heterogeneous in task scope, benchmarks, and validator designs; head‑to‑head, preregistered paired comparisons that isolate verifier marginal benefit in controlled NetOps tasks are limited. Our study complements that literature by providing an artifact‑grounded, preregistered paired analysis isolating verifier effect under a shared‑generation protocol.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and design: The study preregistration (cnsmp2026-llm-verifier-predeployment-001; SHA‑256 recorded in the execution manifest) defined a paired confirmatory design with 300 intent pairs stratified by difficulty (100 low / 100 medium / 100 high). The preregistration included a pilot (n=60) for power calibration; the pilot was not executed and the main N=300 was used as pre‑specified (see Execution Summary). Execution protocol: for each pair the experiment produced a single shared LLM generation (shared_initial) using gpt-5-mini (as recorded in execution/model_configuration.json) and then deterministically derived two episodes: baseline = accept the shared_initial as the baseline episode (no verifier repair); guarded = run deterministic_netops_validator_v5 on the shared_initial and, if it failed, invoke at most one automated repair call and then revalidate. Success definition: an unflagged verifier pass = validator returns valid==true and automated_flag==FALSE under the preregistered scorer rule (full_intent_constraint_validation). Sampling/exclusions: pairs would be excluded only if both condition calls failed due to infrastructure/provider outage; none were excluded. Analysis plan: primary confirmatory test used paired_binary_analysis_v1 (exact McNemar‑equivalent two‑sided test, with a paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI, B=10000, seed=1729). All design choices, exclusion rules, seeds, and analysis executors were frozen in the preregistration.
sections.results: Execution summary (artifact-backed): planned_episode_count=600, completed_episode_count=600, complete_pair_count=300, model_calls_used=301, stage_counts: shared_initial_generation=300, repair=1 (execution_manifest.json and deterministic_reconciliation.json). Marginal outcomes (analysis/condition_summary.csv): baseline successes 299 / 300 (0.9966667), guarded successes 300 / 300 (1.0). Paired contingency (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv): n11=299 (both pass), n10=1 (guarded only), n01=0 (baseline only), n00=0 (both fail). Confirmatory inference (paired_binary_analysis_v1): absolute paired difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.0033333; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; 95% paired bootstrap percentile CI = [0.00, 0.01] (bootstrap_seed=1729, B=10000). Per‑stratum outcomes: sampling was stratified at 100 pairs per stratum (low/medium/high) as preregistered (execution/task_manifest.jsonl). Observed per‑stratum verifier passes were near‑ceiling: baseline passes = low 100/100, medium 100/100, high 99/100 (total 299/300); guarded passes = 100/100 for each stratum (300/300). The single discordant pair (baseline fail → guarded pass) occurred in the high complexity stratum and was resolved by the single permitted automated repair. Contamination and independence checks: deterministic contamination checks reported no flags (analysis/contamination_summary.csv is empty). The task generator produced explicit intents and required sequences; the validator independently enforces full_intent_constraint_validation semantics. While the generator and validator encode related domain semantics, contamination instrumentation detected no evidence of direct coupling that would trivially force pass agreement. Representative artifacts demonstrating the shared_initial protocol and identical shared outputs across conditions are archived (e.g., execution/responses/task-000001-shared-initial.txt, execution/responses/task-000001-baseline.txt, execution/responses/task-000001-guarded.txt). Missingness/exclusions: none.
sections.discussion: Interpretation: On this synthetic suite with the selected model and validator, baseline single‑shot LLM generation was near‑perfect, leaving minimal headroom for the verifier to produce a large absolute improvement. The observed paired improvement (0.33 percentage points) is operationally small and statistically non‑significant under the preregistered test because of the ceiling effect and extremely low discordance. The result illustrates that measurable verifier utility (by this specific estimand) depends strongly on base model quality, task difficulty distribution, and the validator's coverage relative to task semantics. Practical implications: verifiers may still provide deterministic flagging, auditability, and an automated safety net (the single rescued case demonstrates this), but their marginal effect on pass rates can be negligible when prompts and tasks are solvable by the LLM. Threats to validity: (1) Construct validity — the synthetic generator and deterministic validator share high‑level intent semantics; although contamination checks found no flags, this alignment reduces task hardness relative to real‑world heterogeneity. (2) External validity — single model (gpt-5-mini) and single validator evaluated; results may not generalize to weaker models or different validators. (3) Ceiling effect — stratified design produced many easy/solvable tasks for this model prompt pairing. Recommendations: future work should target harder, more diverse, and real operator corpora; evaluate multiple LLM backends and richer/verifier‑diverse validators; measure operational costs (latency, model‑call budget) and human‑in‑the‑loop thresholds.
sections.conclusion: We report a preregistered, fully archived paired comparison of a verifier‑assisted pipeline versus LLM‑only single‑shot generation for pre‑deployment NetOps changes. Using gpt-5-mini and deterministic_netops_validator_v5 on a synthetic topology suite, baseline single‑shot generation achieved 299/300 unflagged verifier passes and the guarded pipeline 300/300, producing a negligible paired improvement (0.00333; exact McNemar p=1.0; 95% CI [0.00,0.01]). The preregistered pilot (n=60) was not executed and the main N=300 was used as pre‑specified. These artifact‑grounded results do not imply verifiers are unnecessary; rather, they show the verifier's measurable incremental benefit depends on model capability, task difficulty, and validator coverage. We release complete preregistration, execution, and analysis artifacts to support community follow‑up under more challenging conditions.

limitations: Synthetic benchmark: tasks and topologies were generated by the preregistered deterministic task generator; real‑world heterogeneity may expose different failure modes and increase verifier marginal utility.
Single model and validator: only gpt-5-mini and deterministic_netops_validator_v5 were evaluated; results may not generalize to other LLMs or richer/verifier‑diverse validators.

Ceiling effect: baseline single‑shot performance was near 100% on this suite (299/300), producing limited discordance and low power to detect small absolute improvements relative to the preregistered target (10 percentage points).
Pilot not executed: the preregistered pilot (n=60) intended for discordance estimation and power calibration was not executed; the main N=300 was used as pre‑specified.
Operational deployment not evaluated: latency, cost, operator workflows, and human‑in‑the‑loop thresholds were outside the confirmatory scope and require further study.
